The Common silver-biddy Gerres oyena is a gerreid fish that inhabits shallow coastal waters and estuarine environments throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Like many members of its family, it undergoes a pelagic larval phase before transitioning to a demersal existence on sandy bottoms and seagrass beds. Neonates emerge from transparent, yolk-laden eggs measuring approximately 0.5 mm in diameter, and the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0000655 grams [Wwb = 0.0000655 grams], reflecting the modest maternal investment typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts. Field surveys and growth-curve analyses indicate that the ultimate standard length attained by this species reaches 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it from several smaller congeneric species that rarely exceed 20 cm. Age-length relationships derived from otolith readings suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic length after several years of steady somatic expansion, with the most rapid gains occurring during the first two years of life when prey resources are abundant and metabolic demands for tissue synthesis are highest.

Reproductive development in Gerres oyena follows a predictable ontogenetic trajectory, with the standard length at puberty estimated at 16.7 centimeters [Lp = 16.7 centimeters], a size that corresponds to roughly midway through the species' ultimate length range. This threshold was determined from histological examination of gonadal tissue, which revealed the onset of active gametogenesis in individuals exceeding that body size. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 70.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 70.5 grams], a mass that reflects the allocation of somatic reserves toward reproductive structures such as developing ovaries and testes. Puberty in this species appears to be size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent, a pattern observed across many iteroparous fishes that must attain a critical body size before energy can be diverted toward egg production and spawning behaviour. In warmer waters within its distribution, individuals may reach this size more quickly, while populations at the cooler edges of the range experience delayed maturation.

Maximum reproductive output in Gerres oyena has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the thermal regime of its preferred habitats. At a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], gravid females produce approximately 1006 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1006 eggs per spawning event], a rate that represents the highest per-spawn fecundity recorded for this species under optimal thermal conditions. Expressed as a daily rate for the reference female of 20.1 cm total length, this corresponds to a reproductive rate at TL 20.1 cm of approximately 1006 eggs per day  at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This value was derived from observations of females with a total length of 20.1 cm, indicating that larger individuals contribute disproportionately to population-level egg production. The spawning season typically extends over several months, with individual females releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs during this period. The per-spawn output corresponds to the maximum reproductive capacity, as spawning frequency may decline under suboptimal temperature regimes or when food availability is reduced. Field studies have confirmed that females at this body size can sustain such output for at least several weeks, suggesting substantial energetic reserves are mobilised to support gamete production.

Adult body mass in Gerres oyena reaches an ultimate wet weight of 378 grams [Wwi = 378 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species across multiple populations. This asymptotic mass represents the maximum recorded weight in fully grown individuals, typically achieved after the completion of somatic growth and the onset of reproductive maturity. The length-weight relationship follows the standard allometric form, with body mass increasing as a power function of standard length, and the exponent indicates a slightly positive allometric growth pattern characteristic of gerreid fishes that accumulate lipid reserves in the abdominal cavity. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Gerres oyena attains a substantially larger body size than Gerres filamentosus, which rarely exceeds 250 grams, but remains smaller than Gerres erythrourus, where individuals can surpass 500 grams. The ultimate wet weight is attained only after several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates, particularly polychaetes and small crustaceans.

Longevity records for Gerres oyena indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3102 days [am = approximately 3102 days] based on mark-recapture studies and validated otolith ageing conducted at an ambient water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This places the species among the longer-lived members of the Gerreidae, a family generally characterised by moderate longevity. The mortality schedule appears to follow a Type II pattern, with relatively constant age-specific mortality rates across most of the adult lifespan, although senescence-related increases in natural mortality become evident after approximately seven years of age. Individuals inhabiting protected estuarine environments with lower predation pressure tend to achieve greater longevity than those on exposed coastal reefs where piscivorous predators are more abundant. The combination of a moderate lifespan, iteroparous reproductive strategy, and relatively high fecundity suggests that population persistence is maintained through a balance of adult survivorship and consistent annual recruitment.
